vignette:
It was a Tuesday evening in late October when the assault happened—almost three years ago now, though for Alan, a fifty-three-year-old tutor, it might as well have been yesterday. A colleague he had trusted, another tutor from the center where he worked, asked him to stay late to discuss a joint student. Alan agreed. When they were alone in the small consultation room, the man’s tone shifted. He told Alan to sit down, and something in the way he said it—flat, unhurried—made Alan obey. What followed was a blur of hands and pressure and a voice saying *just stay still* while Alan’s own body seemed to belong to someone else. He remembered the dry scent of the colleague’s aftershave, the fluorescent light buzzing overhead, the way the chair arm dug into his ribs. He also knew, with a hollow certainty, that there were gaps: moments he could not account for, fragments that felt as though they had been erased. Later, when a police officer asked him to describe what happened, Alan opened his mouth and found no words. He knew what he had endured, but the sounds would not come. He wrote it down instead, and then he burned the paper.

In the months that followed, Alan’s life contracted. He stopped using the tutoring center altogether and began working exclusively from his own home office, which he had arranged carefully: desk against the wall, chair with a clear sightline to the door, windows locked. He took only female students now, and even then he made sure the door remained open. When a new male student’s mother called to schedule an intake session, Alan said he was fully booked. He would not allow himself to be alone with a man he did not know. At first, this felt like simple caution. But the caution deepened into a constant scanning: when he walked into a coffee shop, he took note of every male customer, watching for sudden movements, for someone who might step too close. He chose a seat with a wall at his back, and if that seat was taken he left. He avoided unfamiliar cafés, restaurants, libraries—any place where he could not predict the layout or the exits.

The worst moments came without warning. At a grocery store, a stranger’s hand brushed his arm while reaching for the same box of tea. Alan’s chest went tight, his palms slick, and he abandoned his cart and walked out. He began to order everything online. He stopped shaking hands, even with acquaintances. When a female student leaned across the desk to show him a notebook, he flinched backward. She looked hurt; he could not explain. He felt a gulf opening between himself and everyone else, a glass wall he could not see through from the other side. His only refuge was smoking—he had taken it up again after years of stopping, a cigarette on the back porch at dawn and dusk, the one moment when he did not have to watch anyone.

What frightened Alan most was the sense that his own body had become an enemy. During the assault he had frozen—his limbs would not move, his voice would not cry out. He still woke some mornings believing that if he ever needed to run or fight, his body would betray him again. The vigilance felt necessary: *you never know what can happen next*, he told himself. He kept his eyes moving, assessing, preparing. But it was exhausting. He had stopped seeing old friends because any invitation—dinner, a movie, a walk—carried the risk of being trapped in a situation he could not control. At fifty-three, he had imagined his life settling into comfortable rhythms; instead, he was scheduling his days around invisible threats.

It was his sister who finally pushed him toward help. She had called to say she was worried, that he sounded hollow. Alan did not know how to tell her that he was always watching, that he had not let anyone touch him in three years, that he could picture the fluorescent light and the aftershave in perfect detail but could not speak a single sentence about what had been done to him. He started therapy because he was tired of being so careful. He hoped—though he could not yet say it out loud—that someone might help him find the words, and that once he did, his body might finally let him rest.
